Cool it
KOOL it
phrase (Silent Generation slang)
From Old English col, moderately cold; by Webster’s day cool already meant calm and not excited as well as not hot, and to cool meant to allay passion. Cool it — calm down, stop, take it easy — is American slang recorded by the 1950s, at home both in jazz talk and on the playground, where it was the word for breaking up a quarrel before it became a fight.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Cool it, you two!" was what a big brother said in 1956 when the twins started shoving over the last cookie. It means calm down, back off, stop before this gets worse — and it is wise counsel. Scripture says the same thing in older words: "The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with" (Pro 17:14). A quarrel is like a crack in a dam; the time to stop it is early. James gives the rule for a hot head: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19), "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20). And Proverbs gives the tool: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1). Not all anger is sin — "Be ye angry, and sin not" (Eph 4:26) — but most of ours is hasty and selfish, and it needs cooling. The one who says "cool it" at the right moment is doing the work of a peacemaker, and Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Mat 5:9). The Prince of Peace made peace at the greatest cost, by the blood of His cross. A grandfather can teach the children to cool it with each other, and to be the one in the room who cools things down.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s) for calm down, stop, back off — from the 1828 cool, not excited by passion, and an echo of Solomon’s leave off contention, before it be meddled with (Pro 17:14).

expand to see more

COOL IT, phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Calm down; stop; take it easy. "Cool it, you two — Dad’s trying to sleep."

Webster (1828) — COOL, adjective 1. Moderately cold; being of a temperature between hot and cold; as cool air; cool water. 2. Not ardent or zealous; not angry; not fond; not excited by passion of any kind; indifferent; as a cool friend; a cool temper; a cool lover. COOL, verb transitive 2. To moderate excitement of temper; to allay, as passion of any kind; to calm, as anger; to abate, as love; to moderate, as desire, zeal or ardor; to render indifferent. COOL, verb intransitive 2. To lose the heat of excitement or passion; to become less ardent, angry, zealous, or affectionate; to become more moderate.

Decode for families: "cool it" means "calm down and stop" — good advice in any decade.

Key Scripture

Pro 17:14 — "The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with."

Jas 1:19 — "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:"

Jas 1:20 — "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God."

Pro 15:1 — "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger."

Mat 5:9 — "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

Modern Corruption

A wholesome phrase for making peace; the only cautions are that it can be said with contempt, or used to hush a wrong that ought to be heard.

expand to see more

Cool it is good counsel in two words, and Scripture says much the same. It belongs with the soft answer and the slow tongue. A family that uses it to stop squabbles is using slang for a godly end.

Two small cautions. Said with a sneer, "cool it" can be its own grievous word, stirring up the anger it means to calm (Pro 15:1). And sometimes it is used to silence a person with a real grievance; peacemaking means dealing with the wrong, not burying it. Cool the temper, then hear the complaint.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English col (moderately cold) → cool (calm, not excited by passion, 1828) → 1950s slang cool it (calm down, stop).

1950s American slang: cool it — calm down; stop; take it easy
